questions.q: What is the correct order of the five-part executive presentation?
questions.explain: Lead with the verdict, support it with a little evidence, acknowledge risk, state the ask, and close with what you'll do this week.

questions.q: With $5.2M won and $6.0M of open pipeline at a 27% win rate, what is the rough forecast?
options: About $6.8M, roughly $1.2M short of an $8.0M target
questions.explain: $6.0M x 27% is about $1.6M. Added to $5.2M won, that is roughly $6.8M, or about $1.2M below the $8.0M target.

questions.q: Why is 2.1x pipeline coverage less reassuring at a 27% win rate?
options: Win rate has no relationship to coverage
At a 27% win rate you would need roughly 3.7x coverage to expect to close the gap
questions.explain: If only about 27% of pipeline closes, covering the gap takes roughly 1 divided by 0.27, or about 3.7x. So 2.1x looks comfortable but is not.

questions.q: What assumption should you state when applying the count-based win rate to pipeline dollars?
options: That deal size does not matter
That it is a rough rule, not a forecast model, since deals differ in size and stage
That Data Cloud has already predicted the outcome
questions.explain: A count-based rate ignores differences in deal size and stage. Naming that limit builds credibility and signals sound judgment.

questions.q: Which portfolio practice best proves your own work?
options: Hiding limits so the project looks flawless
Using your own screenshots from your own org, labeled as sample data, and stating limits plainly
questions.explain: Your own labeled screenshots demonstrate real work. Stated limits show judgment. Borrowed screenshots and hidden gaps undermine trust.
